content: Zidovudine injection has the potential to cause serious side effects, including liver damage, blood toxicities, and muscle disorders. If you experience symptoms such as unusual breathing, shortness of breath, unusual bleeding or bruising, extreme tiredness or weakness, pale skin, fever, chills, sore throat, fatigue, loss of appetite, upset stomach, vomiting, dark urine, yellowing of the skin, pale stools, muscle weakness, lack of strength, or muscle pain, you should contact your doctor immediately. It is essential to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. Your doctor will order specific lab tests to monitor your response to zidovudine. Your doctor has prescribed zidovudine, an antiviral medication, to help treat your infection. This medication will be administered intravenously, added to a fluid that will drip through a needle or catheter placed in your vein for at least 60 minutes every 4 hours. Zidovudine is used either alone or in combination with other medications to treat human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection in patients with or without acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). It works by slowing the spread of HIV in the body. However, zidovudine is not a cure for HIV and may not reduce the number of HIV-related illnesses. Additionally, it does not prevent the transmission of HIV to others. This medication may also be prescribed for other uses; consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Your healthcare provider may assess the effectiveness and side effects of your treatment through laboratory tests and physical examinations. It is crucial to keep all appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. The duration of your treatment will depend on how your infection and symptoms respond to the medication. Before starting zidovudine, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to zidovudine or any other drugs. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications you are taking, especially acetaminophen, acyclovir (Zovirax), aspirin, cancer chemotherapy, cimetidine (Tagamet), fluconazole (Diflucan), foscarnet (Foscavir), ganciclovir (Cytovene), indomethacin (Indocin), interferon, lorazepam (Ativan), oxazepam (Serax), probenecid (Benemid), valproic acid (Depakene, Depakote), and vitamins. Inform your doctor if you have or have ever had liver or kidney disease, muscle diseases or swelling, anemia, a history of alcohol abuse, or any bleeding or blood-related problems. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, notify your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking zidovudine, contact your doctor immediately. Additionally, inform your doctor if you consume alcohol. Before administering zidovudine, inspect the solution carefully. It should be clear and free of floating particles. Gently squeeze the bag or check the container to ensure there are no leaks. Do not use the solution if it is discolored, contains particles, or if the bag or container is leaking. Use a new solution, but show the damaged one to your healthcare provider. It is critical to use your medication exactly as directed. Do not stop your therapy on your own for any reason, as this could worsen your infection and lead to hospitalization. Do not alter your dosing schedule without consulting your healthcare provider. If you encounter a mechanical problem, such as a blockage in the tubing, needle, or catheter, your healthcare provider may instruct you to stop the infusion. If this occurs, contact your healthcare provider immediately to ensure your therapy continues. Mild side effects of zidovudine are common. Notify your doctor if any of the following symptoms are severe or persistent: stomach pain, diarrhea or loose stools, constipation, headache, dizziness, or difficulty sleeping. If you experience a rash or any of the severe side effects listed in the important warning section, contact your doctor immediately. Serious side effects should also be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Your healthcare provider may provide you with a two-day supply of zidovudine at a time. You will be instructed to store it in the refrigerator. Take your next dose out of the refrigerator one hour before use and place it in a clean, dry area to allow it to warm to room temperature. Store your medication only as directed and ensure you understand the proper storage requirements. Keep your supplies in a clean, dry place when not in use, and keep all medications and supplies out of the reach of children. Your healthcare provider will instruct you on how to safely dispose of used needles, syringes, tubing, and containers to prevent accidental injury. In the event of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. If you are receiving zidovudine intravenously or subcutaneously, it is important to recognize the symptoms of a catheter-related infection, which occurs at the site where the needle enters your vein or skin.
